t: Doug Hurley and I are about to take NASA's SpaceX, uh, Demo-2 mission to the International Space Station.
Uh, during that mission, we'll, uh, uh, perform some check-outs.
Uh, Doug will get a chance to do some flying, actually, of the vehicle close to the International Space Station, for example.
And we'll make sure all those systems are working for future missions that might not necessarily exercise all those different features of the vehicle.
The fundamental purpose of the Demo-2 mission is to get certification for, uh, uh, future, uh, missions from, uh, SpaceX to the International Space Station rotating crew, uh,
to meet NASA's needs aboard the Space Station.
The SpaceX vehicle, uh, has a lot of features and capabilities that, uh, hopefully we never have to utilize in a real mission, uh, but Doug and I will make sure that they are all ready,
just in case we do.
And, uh, it's everything from, uh, a response to a fire on board, uh, to, uh, flying close to the, uh, International Space Station manually instead of letting the computer do it.
We'll make sure all those systems are working, uh, during the test flight, so that the future missions, uh, will have 'em available, even if they don't plan to utilize 'em.
Absolutely, we've got a lot of objectives, uh, onboard the, uh, vehicle that we need to accomplish to really make sure that it's, uh, good to go.
Uh, we'll do everything from actually talk from the Dragon vehicle to a Russian Soyuz, uh, once we get a closer dock to the International Space Station,
just to make sure that comm system was, uh, working.

If you ever needed it to-- during an emergency, we'll, uh, take the spacesuits on and off in a couple of different, uh, situations to make sure that we have, uh, good data for how long that takes if you had to do it from an emergency response perspective.

We'll dig out all kinds of hardware that's stowed in the, uh, nooks and crannies of the vehicle so that we have a-a good feel for how things are in place and, uh, getting them back in place, uh, prior to entry.

And so we, uh, plan to do all those things as a-- just a part of our test mission, so missions in the future can focus on the real mission, which is getting trained crews to the International Space Station.
You know, as we get, uh, closer and closer to the launch date, we've had to balance, uh, a lot of things.
We've had to, uh, accept kind of the status of the vehicle and then, uh, understand how we're gonna operate it.
And I think really both Doug and I's focus is making sure that, uh, we're proficient, uh, for whatever launch dates come.
We've had the launch date kinda, uh, slip a little bit to this point.
And so we're really chasing the final-final preparations to make sure that we're, uh, on time and on target for the launch date right now, which is, uh, in late May.
You know, there's-- there are parts of it-- of the mission that are discovery, and there are parts of it that aren't, right?
And so you just want to know which parts are in the discovery portion of things, which part is exploration, and which part your-- you know, in our case,
we're-we're providing a vehicle to, uh, future crews.
And so our intent is to make that vehicle predictable and-and I-- and figure out everything so that we can come back and tell them, so that the-the vehicle itself is predictable,
even though the mission itself might not be, right?
So, um...

Maybe it's a complicated way to describe it, but, uh, you know, you want Dragon's vehicle response to be predictable, so that when we-- we can use that to discover things with the International Space Station.
Our intent is to not, you know, try to, uh, explore the Mach envelope for a capsule coming through the atmosphere, necessarily.
You know, and-and-and see whether or not that was, uh, a limit that, you know, human wise, we could tolerate or we couldn't tolerate sort of a thing.
Our intent is to provide this vehicle to enable the-- the real exploration mission, which in this case is keeping the Space Station, uh, operating,
keeping the scientific discoveries, uh, even the-the human piece of that with, uh-- with crew members on orbit for extended duration, keep that data continuing to come.
That's what we're providing with this vehicle.
Our-our goal is to-- is to-to-to not necessarily have every aspect of the-the vehicle's performance be an exploration objective,
you know, 'cause we're focused on a different real exp-- exploration objective with the International Space Station.
I think that the mission that we have in front of us and the-the success that we're gonna have is a representation of America.
Um, bringing it back to the Florida coast is, uh, uh, a really, really cool thing.
Just to see how many people from across the country have to pull together to pull something like this off is just a-- it's inspiring to me, and-and I'm just excited to be a part of it.
